title: Psalms Chapter 69 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Psalms chapter 69 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Psalms Chapter 69 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Psalms Chapter 69.

questions.question: In Psalms 69, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: I am become a stranger unto my brethren,
When I wept, and chastened my soul with fasting,
Let not them that wait on thee, O Lord GOD of hosts,
questions.explanation: The phrase 'Save me, O God;' appears first in Psalms 69:1.

questions.question: What has come in unto David's soul?
questions.explanation: David states 'for the waters are come in unto my soul' in Psalms 69:1.

questions.question: Where does David say he sinks?
questions.explanation: David mentions 'I am come into deep waters' in Psalms 69:2.

questions.question: How does David describe his crying?
questions.explanation: David expresses 'I am weary of my crying' in Psalms 69:3.

questions.question: What has covered David's face?
questions.explanation: David states 'shame hath covered my face' in Psalms 69:7.

questions.question: What has David become to his mother's children?
questions.explanation: David says 'I am become a stranger unto my brethren' in Psalms 69:8.

questions.question: What has eaten David up?
questions.explanation: David mentions 'For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up' in Psalms 69:9.

questions.question: What did David wear as a garment?
questions.explanation: David states 'I made sackcloth also my garment' in Psalms 69:11.

questions.question: What do those who sit in the gate do?
questions.explanation: David mentions 'They that sit in the gate speak against me' in Psalms 69:12.

questions.question: What is David's throat described as?
questions.explanation: David states 'my throat is dried' in Psalms 69:3.

questions.question: Because of whom has David borne reproach?
questions.explanation: David states 'Because for thy sake I have borne reproach' in Psalms 69:7.

questions.question: True or False: David feels alienated from his mother's children.
questions.explanation: David says 'I am become a stranger unto my brethren, and an alien unto my mother's children' in Psalms 69:8.

questions.question: True or False: David's sins are known to God.
questions.explanation: David states 'O God, thou knowest my foolishness; and my sins are not hid from thee' in Psalms 69:5.

questions.question: True or False: David claims he is the song of the angels.
questions.explanation: The text does not say David is the song of the angels; it states 'I was the song of the drunkards' in Psalms 69:12.

questions.question: True or False: David restored what he took away.
questions.explanation: David states 'then I restored that which I took not away' in Psalms 69:4, indicating he did not restore what he took away.

medium.title: Psalms Chapter 69 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Psalms Chapter 69 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What does the psalmist ask God to do in Psalms 69:14?
options: Deliver me out of the mire
questions.correctAnswer: Deliver me out of the mire
questions.explanation: The psalmist specifically asks God to 'Deliver me out of the mire' in Psalms 69:14, expressing a plea for rescue from distress.

questions.question: What does Psalms 69:13 promise will happen if someone prays to God in an acceptable time?
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:13 indicates that the psalmist's prayer is directed to God, who is implored to hear him in the multitude of His mercy, suggesting that God will respond favorably.

questions.question: What does the psalmist ask God not to let happen in Psalms 69:15?
questions.explanation: The psalmist explicitly requests in Psalms 69:15 that God not allow the waterflood to overflow him, signifying a plea for protection from overwhelming trouble.

questions.question: According to Psalms 69:16, why should God turn to the psalmist?
options: Because of the psalmist's good deeds
Because of His goodness and mercy
questions.correctAnswer: Because of His goodness and mercy
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:16 states that the psalmist appeals to God's lovingkindness and multitude of tender mercies as reasons for Him to turn and help.

questions.question: What emotional state does the psalmist express in Psalms 69:20?
questions.explanation: The psalmist describes being 'full of heaviness' in Psalms 69:20, indicating deep emotional distress and sorrow over his reproach.

questions.question: What does the psalmist request in Psalms 69:18?
options: Draw nigh unto my soul and redeem it
questions.correctAnswer: Draw nigh unto my soul and redeem it
questions.explanation: In Psalms 69:18, the psalmist seeks God's presence and redemption, showing his dependence on God for deliverance from his enemies.

questions.question: What does Psalms 69:19 indicate about the psalmist's adversaries?
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:19 mentions that God knows the psalmist's reproach and dishonor, indicating that God is aware of the psalmist's struggles with his adversaries.

questions.question: What did the psalmist receive instead of comfort in Psalms 69:21?
options: Gall for meat and vinegar to drink
questions.correctAnswer: Gall for meat and vinegar to drink
questions.explanation: In Psalms 69:21, the psalmist describes receiving gall for food and vinegar for drink, symbolizing rejection and suffering instead of compassion.

questions.question: According to Psalms 69:22, what should happen to their table?
options: It should be full of food
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:22 states that the psalmist desires that their table become a snare, implying a reversal of expected blessings to a trap for the wicked.

questions.question: What does Psalms 69:23 ask God to do to their eyes?
questions.explanation: The psalmist in Psalms 69:23 requests that God darken their eyes so they cannot see, suggesting a plea for divine judgment against his adversaries.

questions.question: What emotion does the psalmist feel in Psalms 69:17?
questions.explanation: The psalmist expresses a sense of urgency and desperation in Psalms 69:17, asking God not to hide His face from him during his trouble.

questions.question: What is the psalmist's main request throughout Psalms 69?
options: To be lifted up in pride
questions.explanation: The overarching theme of Psalms 69 is the psalmist's plea for deliverance from his troubles and enemies, as seen in several verses.

questions.question: True or False: The psalmist expresses confidence in God's mercy in Psalms 69:13.
questions.explanation: The psalmist expresses confidence in God's mercy in Psalms 69:13 by praying for God to hear him based on His multitude of mercy.

questions.question: True or False: The psalmist believes his enemies have treated him fairly according to Psalms 69:4.
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:4 indicates that the psalmist feels wronged, stating that his enemies hate him without cause, which suggests unfair treatment.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 69:24 calls for God's indignation against the psalmist's enemies.
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:24 explicitly asks God to pour out His indignation upon the psalmist's foes, indicating a call for divine anger against them.

hard.title: Psalms Chapter 69 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Psalms Chapter 69.

questions.question: What does the psalmist ask regarding the habitation of his enemies?
questions.explanation: The psalmist asks for their habitation to be desolate in Psalms 69:25, indicating a desire for their destruction.

questions.question: What do the enemies do to the one whom God has smitten?
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:26 states that they persecute him whom God has smitten, showing their malicious intent.

questions.question: What is the psalmist's condition in Psalms 69:29?
questions.explanation: In Psalms 69:29, the psalmist expresses his state of being poor and sorrowful, contrasting with his plea for salvation.

questions.question: In Psalms 69:30, how does the psalmist plan to praise God?
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:30 reveals that the psalmist will praise God with a song and magnify Him with thanksgiving.

questions.question: Who does the LORD hear according to Psalms 69:33?
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:33 states that the LORD hears the poor, emphasizing His concern for the downtrodden.

questions.question: What is promised to those who love God's name in Psalms 69:36?
options: They will be honored by all
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:36 assures that those who love God's name shall dwell in Zion, reflecting God's promise of security.

questions.question: What does the Hebrew word 'mire' in Psalms 69:2 mean?
questions.explanation: The Hebrew word for 'mire' in Psalms 69:2 refers to mud or swamp, indicating the psalmist's desperate situation.

questions.question: What literary device is used in Psalms 69:30, where the psalmist mentions praising with a song?
questions.explanation: The use of 'praise' and 'magnify' in Psalms 69:30 demonstrates parallelism, a common Hebrew poetic structure.

questions.question: Which other Bible passage connects to the theme of God hearing the poor as stated in Psalms 69:33?
questions.explanation: Luke 6:20 states, 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God,' echoing the theme from Psalms 69:33.

questions.question: Which other Bible passage connects to the idea of being blotted out from the book of the living as mentioned in Psalms 69:28?
questions.explanation: Exodus 32:32-33 highlights the concept of being blotted out from God's book, similar to the sentiment in Psalms 69:28.

questions.question: What comes immediately before Psalms 69:30?
options: Let them not come into thy righteousness
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:29, which precedes Psalms 69:30, states 'But I am poor and sorrowful,' setting the stage for the following praise.

questions.question: What comes immediately after Psalms 69:34?
options: Let the heaven and earth praise him
I will praise the name of God
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:35 follows Psalms 69:34, where it speaks of God's promise to save Zion, providing a sense of hope.

questions.question: The psalmist expresses sorrow and a plea for help in Psalms 69:1. What is the nature of this plea?
questions.explanation: In Psalms 69:1, the psalmist cries out for salvation, indicating his desperation and need for divine intervention.

questions.question: The psalmist's adversaries are described in Psalms 69:4. Do they have a valid cause against him?
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:4 states that they hate him without a cause, meaning their animosity is unjustified.

questions.question: The psalmist's condition is one of despair throughout the chapter. Is this an accurate depiction of his emotional state?
questions.explanation: The psalmist consistently expresses despair and sorrow throughout the chapter, highlighting his emotional turmoil.

theological.title: Psalms Chapter 69 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Psalms Chapter 69 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Psalms 69:5 teach about God's knowledge of human sin?
options: God has complete knowledge of human foolishness and sin
God overlooks human sin to show mercy
God is unaware of human folly until confessed
God punishes only the sins that are public
questions.correctAnswer: God has complete knowledge of human foolishness and sin
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:5 states, 'O God, thou knowest my foolishness; and my sins are not hid from thee,' affirming God's omniscient awareness of all human sin, both hidden and apparent.

questions.question: What doctrine about sanctification is taught in Psalms 69:9?
options: Zeal for God's house consumes the believer, uniting suffering with God's reproach
Sanctification is a painless process free from reproach
Believers are called to isolate themselves from reproach
Sanctification is only about moral perfection without suffering
questions.correctAnswer: Zeal for God's house consumes the believer, uniting suffering with God's reproach
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:9 says, 'For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me,' teaching that sanctification involves passionate devotion to God that may result in suffering on His behalf.

questions.question: What doctrine about salvation does Psalms 69:33 teach?
options: The LORD hears the poor and does not despise those in captivity
Salvation is only for the wealthy and free
God ignores the cries of the oppressed
Salvation is earned by human effort
questions.correctAnswer: The LORD hears the poor and does not despise those in captivity
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:33 states, 'For the LORD heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners,' affirming God's salvific concern and attention to the lowly and oppressed.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 69:16 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:16 says, 'Hear me, O LORD; for thy lovingkindness is good,' demonstrating God's attribute of lovingkindness or steadfast love toward His people.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 69:19 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:19 states, 'Thou hast known my reproach, and my shame, and my dishonour: mine adversaries are all before thee,' revealing God's omniscient knowledge of all circumstances.

questions.question: How does Psalms 69:21 connect to the New Testament portrayal of Christ's suffering?
options: It prefigures Jesus being offered vinegar to drink on the cross
It describes the Last Supper institution
It symbolizes the pouring out of the Holy Spirit
questions.correctAnswer: It prefigures Jesus being offered vinegar to drink on the cross
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:21 says, 'They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink,' which is fulfilled in the crucifixion narratives (cf. John 19:29), connecting the Psalm to Christ's sufferings.

questions.question: How does Psalms 69:35 prepare for the eschatological hope found elsewhere in Scripture?
options: It anticipates God's ultimate salvation and restoration of Zion
It predicts the destruction of Jerusalem with no restoration
It denies any future inheritance for God's servants
It emphasizes human effort over divine salvation
questions.correctAnswer: It anticipates God's ultimate salvation and restoration of Zion
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:35 proclaims, 'For God will save Zion, and will build the cities of Judah,' pointing forward to the eschatological fulfillment of God's kingdom restoration (cf. Isaiah 65:17-25).

questions.question: What combined doctrine do verses Psalms 69:13 and Psalms 69:16 teach about God's mercy and timing in salvation?
options: God hears prayers in an acceptable time and responds with abundant tender mercies
God delays hearing prayers and withholds mercy
God's mercy is conditional on human works alone
God's timing is irrelevant to salvation
questions.correctAnswer: God hears prayers in an acceptable time and responds with abundant tender mercies
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:13 and 69:16 together emphasize that God hears prayer 'in an acceptable time' and acts according to 'the multitude of thy tender mercies,' revealing His compassionate responsiveness.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 69:22 and Psalms 69:27 teach about divine judgment on the wicked?
options: God calls for increasing iniquity upon the wicked and their plans to become traps for themselves
God ignores the wicked and their schemes
God rewards the wicked for their cunning
God allows the wicked to enter His righteousness without repentance
questions.correctAnswer: God calls for increasing iniquity upon the wicked and their plans to become traps for themselves
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:22 says, 'Let their table become a snare,' and 69:27 says, 'Add iniquity unto their iniquity,' teaching that God's judgment entails the intensification of the wicked's guilt and self-destruction.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 69:1 and Psalms 69:14 teach about human desperation and divine deliverance?
options: The psalmist's soul is overwhelmed like drowning in deep waters, and he pleads for God to save and not let him sink
Human desperation is futile because God does not intervene
Divine deliverance is earned by human strength alone
The psalmist is indifferent to his circumstances and does not seek help
questions.correctAnswer: The psalmist's soul is overwhelmed like drowning in deep waters, and he pleads for God to save and not let him sink
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:1 says, 'Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul,' and 69:14 pleads, 'Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink,' illustrating the doctrine of human helplessness and the necessity of divine rescue.

questions.question: Sceptics claim that Psalms 69:20-21 promotes a vengeful curse on enemies. What does this passage actually teach?
options: It expresses the psalmist’s deep suffering and plea for God’s justice against persecutors
It instructs believers to personally retaliate against enemies with curses
It denies that the psalmist experienced any real suffering
It teaches that God is indifferent to injustice
questions.correctAnswer: It expresses the psalmist’s deep suffering and plea for God’s justice against persecutors
questions.explanation: Verses 20-21 describe the psalmist's broken heart and the giving of gall and vinegar, symbolizing intense suffering and a prayer for divine justice, not personal vengeance.

questions.question: What doctrine about God’s faithfulness is taught in Psalms 69:36?
options: God’s servants’ descendants will inherit the land and dwell securely
God abandons His servants and their seed
Inheritance is based on human merit alone
God’s promises are conditional on political success
questions.correctAnswer: God’s servants’ descendants will inherit the land and dwell securely
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:36 says, 'The seed also of his servants shall inherit it: and they that love his name shall dwell therein,' affirming God’s covenant faithfulness to His people across generations.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is most clearly demonstrated in Psalms 69:17?
options: God’s readiness to hear and respond to distress
questions.correctAnswer: God’s readiness to hear and respond to distress
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:17 says, 'Hear me speedily,' indicating God’s attribute of being near and responsive to His servant’s troubles.

questions.question: What combined doctrine about human suffering and divine presence do Psalms 69:8 and Psalms 69:18 teach?
options: Even when alienated from kin, the soul can be redeemed through God’s nearness and deliverance
Alienation from family means God has abandoned the sufferer
Human suffering is irrelevant to God’s redemptive work
Redemption depends on human social status
questions.correctAnswer: Even when alienated from kin, the soul can be redeemed through God’s nearness and deliverance
questions.explanation: Verse 8 speaks of alienation, 'I am become a stranger unto my brethren,' while verse 18 pleads, 'Draw nigh unto my soul, and redeem it,' teaching that divine presence and redemption transcend human isolation.

questions.question: How does Psalms 69:30-31 teach about the proper form of worship and sacrifice?
options: God prefers praise and thanksgiving over animal sacrifices
God demands only burnt offerings with no praise
Sacrifices without costly offerings are unacceptable
Worship is only about external rituals
questions.correctAnswer: God prefers praise and thanksgiving over animal sacrifices
questions.explanation: Psalms 69:30-31 state that praising God and thanksgiving 'shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock,' emphasizing heartfelt worship over ritual sacrifice.
